cards.q: Four scales of measurement: list all
cards.a: Nominal; ordinal; interval; ratio
Mode only

cards.q: Ordinal data: why the mean is not used
cards.a: Ranks cannot be added; use median or mode

cards.q: Interval scale: why ratios are not valid
cards.a: No true zero

cards.q: Ratio scale: what it adds to interval scale
cards.a: True zero; ratios and coefficient of variation are valid

cards.q: Scale that is parametric (with interval and ratio data)
cards.a: Interval and ratio; nominal and ordinal are non-parametric
Weight or height
Any value on a scale, subdivided indefinitely (e.g. litres of fuel, temperature)
Fixed countable values (e.g. number of heads in 100 flips)
Measured numerically; calculations can be performed
Describe attributes; observed, not computed; more exploratory
Sum of values divided by their number
Middle value of ordered data
Most frequent value

cards.q: When the median is the better summary
cards.a: When outliers are present (median resists them)
Equal to the mean and median
Spread of values around the mean

cards.q: Steps to calculate SD: list in order
cards.a: Find mean; find deviations; square and sum them; divide by n - 1 (variance); take square root

cards.q: Why sample variance is divided by n - 1
cards.a: Average of sample variances over all samples then equals the population variance (unbiased estimate)

cards.q: Normal distribution: mean plus or minus 1 SD covers
cards.a: 68% of values

cards.q: Normal distribution: mean plus or minus 2 SD covers
cards.a: 95% of values

cards.q: Standard error of the mean (SEM): what it is
cards.a: SD of the sampling distribution of means
SD divided by the square root of n

cards.q: Effect of larger sample size on SEM
cards.a: SEM falls
Proportion of a population with a condition at a given time: old and new cases over population
Cross-sectional; old and new cases both counted in the numerator
Population size at one point in time
Average population over the period, or the mid-period population
New cases only, over a period, in those initially disease-free
Risk of becoming a case in a stated period; ranges 0 to 1

cards.q: Incidence proportion can be measured in which study group
cards.a: Closed cohort only, with the follow-up time stated
Person-time at risk; unit of time must be stated
0 to infinity
Odds of exposure in cases divided by odds of exposure in controls

cards.q: Odds ratio from a 2x2 table (a, b = cases; c, d = controls)
cards.a: OR = ad / bc
No association between exposure and outcome
Exposure is positively associated with the outcome

cards.q: When the odds ratio approximates relative risk
cards.a: When the outcome occurs in less than 10% of the non-exposed population

cards.q: When the odds ratio overestimates relative risk
cards.a: When the outcome is more than 10% in the non-exposed
Risk in exposed divided by risk in unexposed

cards.q: Study design from which relative risk is directly determined
cards.a: Cohort study
Number of patients to treat for one to show a defined effect, beneficial or harmful

cards.q: Why NNT is more informative than relative risk reduction
cards.a: It depends on baseline risk; the same relative reduction gives different NNTs
Probability of the observed result, or more extreme, if the null hypothesis is true

cards.q: Decision rule for the null hypothesis
cards.a: Reject H0 if P is less than the chosen significance level
No evidence against the null hypothesis
Weak evidence against the null hypothesis
Moderate evidence against the null hypothesis
Very strong evidence against the null hypothesis
No difference between sample and population, or between samples; can be rejected, never proved
A difference exists (greater, smaller or simply different)

cards.q: Steps of hypothesis testing: list in order
cards.a: Set H0 and H1; check assumptions; fix alpha (usually 5%); apply test statistic; decide (P 0.05 or less rejects H0)

cards.q: 95% confidence interval for a large sample
cards.a: Mean plus or minus 1.96 standard errors

cards.q: Advantage of a confidence interval over a P value alone
cards.a: Shows direction, size and precision of the effect

cards.q: Four outcomes of a hypothesis test: list all
cards.a: Correct retention (1 - alpha); type I error, false positive (alpha); type II error, false negative (beta); correct rejection (power, 1 - beta)
Beta
Use as large a random sample as possible; interpret at the pre-set significance level

cards.q: Which error Sarkar calls more serious in medical research
cards.a: Type I error (false positive)

cards.q: Sample size below which the t test replaces the Z test
cards.a: Less than 30

cards.q: Who first described the t distribution
cards.a: Gosset (pen-name 'Student')

cards.q: Types of t test: list all
cards.a: Unpaired (independent samples); paired (same group at two times); one-sample (group mean against known mean)

cards.q: Degrees of freedom: unpaired t test
Degrees of freedom: paired t test

cards.a: Comparing means of more than two groups; repeated t tests are unreliable
One-way; two-way; factorial; repeated measures

cards.q: Two-way ANOVA: how many factors and what they must be
cards.a: Two categorical independent variables; one continuous dependent variable
Tests two factors at the same time, and their independence if each cell has more than one observation

cards.q: Factorial ANOVA: what it gives beyond the main effects
cards.a: Information on interaction (dependence or independence of the factors)

cards.q: 2 x 2 factorial design: number of treatment groups
cards.a: Four

cards.q: Repeated measures ANOVA: equivalent of which test
cards.a: One-way ANOVA for related groups; extension of the dependent t test
F ratio: between-group mean square divided by within-group mean square
Each group from a normal population; equal variances; independent samples; random observations
Non-parametric test for categorical (frequency) data; developed by Karl Pearson
Test of proportion; test of association between attributes; goodness of fit
(rows - 1) x (columns - 1)

cards.q: Parametric tests: distribution assumed and measure used
cards.a: Normal distribution; use the mean

cards.q: Non-parametric tests: data and measure used
cards.a: Ordinal or ranked data; use the median; no distribution assumed

cards.q: Power of parametric versus non-parametric tests
cards.a: Parametric tests have more statistical power

cards.q: Sample size for a one-sample t test to tolerate skewed data (Sarkar)
cards.a: More than 20

cards.q: Sample size per group for a two-sample t test to tolerate skewed data (Sarkar)
cards.a: More than 15 per group
Lower power, so higher risk of type II error
The mean is the better measure and the sample is large
The median is the better measure, whatever the sample size
Statistical analysis integrating findings of many studies (Glass, 1976)

cards.q: Steps of a meta-analysis: list in order
cards.a: Define the question as PICO(T); search databases and grey literature; screen abstracts and full papers; extract data; pool and analyse
Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Time
Greater statistical power and precision from large pooled data; resolves conflicting results; analyses harms and subgroups; considered evidence-based
Hard to find appropriate studies; needs experienced reviewers and quality rating; published articles may lack data; advanced statistics; heterogeneity can bias results

cards.q: Forest plot: what the horizontal axis shows
cards.a: Effect measure (OR, RR, risk difference, SMD)
Study weight
Pooled estimate (centre) and its 95% CI (width)

cards.q: Forest plot: a result is non-significant when
cards.a: The diamond or a study's CI crosses the line of no effect
Best research evidence, critically appraised, combined with clinical skill and patient preference
Better outcomes, less harm, better cost-effectiveness and shared decisions

cards.q: Search engine named for evidence in EBM
cards.a: TRIP (Turning Research Into Practice) database

cards.q: Five steps of critical appraisal: list in order
cards.a: Ask an answerable (PICO) question; search for evidence; appraise methodology and design; appraise results; judge significance and impact
Randomised controlled trials (25-item checklist)
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (27 items)
Observational studies: cohort, case-control and cross-sectional
Meta-analyses of observational studies (35-item checklist)
Diagnostic or prognostic accuracy studies (25 items)
Trial protocols (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials)

cards.q: Components of a research protocol, Part A (science): list all
cards.a: Summary; rationale and objectives; design, population and criteria; methodology with randomisation, blinding and stopping rules

cards.q: Components of a research protocol, Part A (conduct): list all
cards.a: Safety and adverse-event reporting; data management and sample size; quality assurance; expected outcomes and publication; timeline and team; ethics

cards.q: Common types of randomisation: list all
cards.a: Simple; systematic; stratified; multistage; cluster; multiphase; block; unequal; minimisation
Removes selection bias (with allocation concealment); balances known and unknown factors between groups

cards.q: Criteria of a good randomisation method
cards.a: Unpredictable; produces balanced groups; simple to use
Equalises numbers in each arm; balance holds even if the trial stops early

cards.q: Block randomisation: problem with fixed blocks
cards.a: Staff may predict the next assignment
Adaptive stratified allocation (Pocock and Simon) that reduces imbalance between arms
Natural groups such as villages, wards, schools or factories

cards.q: Cluster sampling for immunisation coverage: number of clusters and children
cards.a: 30 clusters; 7 children each; 210 children
Less expensive than other methods
Higher sampling error than other techniques
Absolute efficacy of the test drug (identical dummy treatment)

cards.q: Placebo control: when not to use it
cards.a: When an available treatment is known to prevent serious harm such as death or irreversible morbidity
Where blinding is not feasible; cannot be fully blinded

cards.q: Active control trial: why it poses fewer ethical problems
cards.a: All subjects receive active treatment

cards.q: Very small study (about 50 participants), single centre: randomisation method
cards.a: Adaptive minimisation

cards.q: Trial funding risk noted in Sarkar
cards.a: Industry funding of RCTs can create conflict of interest that may influence results

cards.q: CONSORT 2010 checklist items for parallel-group randomised trials
cards.a: 25 items

cards.a: Probability of migraine pain relief against hours after dosing
10 mg rizatriptan vs placebo

cards.a: Falls; SE = SD divided by the square root of n

cards.q: Where the sample size calculation is stated in a trial report
cards.a: Methods section

cards.q: Result of an inadequate sample size calculation
cards.a: False-negative results

cards.q: Power usually accepted for a clinical trial
cards.a: 0.8 to 0.9 (80-90% chance of detecting a real effect)

cards.q: Relative seriousness of type II vs type I error
cards.a: Type II is regarded more leniently

cards.q: Subjects needed to detect a 50% to 40% mortality fall (p<0.05, power 0.9)
cards.a: About 850

cards.q: Patients exposed before the first case of a 1-in-10,000 toxicity
cards.a: Several hundred thousand

cards.q: Where rare drug toxicities are first detected
cards.a: Phase 4, after marketing

cards.q: Effect of a larger trial on the smallest detectable relative risk
cards.a: A smaller relative risk becomes detectable
